newsitem.title: SPAIN: FEATURE - Telefonica seen fit to face competitors.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Telefonica seen fit to face competitors.

text.p: Spain's telecommunications giant Telefonica, which will pass entirely into private hands next month, is seen as lean and mean enough to face competition despite years of coddling as a de facto monopoly, experts say.

The company has been thrust in the spotlight with the state's sale of its remaining 21 percent stake on February 18, and it is proving to be a heavyweight when put up against other European telecoms operators being sold off at the same time.

Investors believe Telefonica de Espana, with its experience answering to shareholders and extensive Latin American investments to offset potential domestic market loss, has an edge over other European telecoms operators.

"Telefonica offers the most diversified sources of earnings of any of the European telcos," a report by one foreign investment house said. "It has been singularly successful at reducing its relative dependence on domestic telco earnings."
EVEN RIVALS ADMIRE AGILITY
Even its rivals in Spain's young advanced services markets admire the ability of the former monopoly to put up a fight.

"Telefonica is an agile, aggressive competitor able to react in a liberalised market," said Ignacio Sanchez, managing director of Airtel, which vies with Telefonica in mobile phones. "We have to deal with them and they're a true competitor."
Airtel's appearance as the first competitor in cellular phones woke up the market to bring Spain's penetration rate up to 7.0 percent from 2.7 percent in just over a year.
The second mobile license holder is a consortium of banks including Banco Central Hispano and Banco Santander, industrial partners and international operators Airtouch and British Telecommunications.
Sanchez sees the market reaching 11 percent penetration, with Airtel claiming one-third, by the time its duopoly with Telefonica faces a third licensed mobile phone operator in 1998.

While Telefonica, which had been listlessly offering a cellular service, responded to the challenge of competition with aggressive marketing and new technology, the jury is still out on whether it can do the same in more crucial core operations.
COBWEBS OF MONOPOLY SWEPT AWAY
Telefonica's new chairman, Juan Villalonga, insists he is sweeping away the cobwebs of monopoly with a fresh new corporate culture aimed at pleasing the customers and the shareholders.
"We've got a new, remodelled organisation," he told investors at a recent presentation of the share offer. "Our primary message is that we're going to maximise value for shareholders."
Telefonica's new attitude coincided with the arrival of a conservative government, which abandoned an initial protectionist attitude in the sector for one favouring full liberalisation.

The conservatives, under Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, swept a long overdue cable law into effect, cut phone tariffs, set up an independent regulator and created a duopoly in basic voice service with state broadcaster Retevision.
The sense of relief in the industry is palpable. At business gatherings and conferences, there is a buzz of activity as Spain gets connected after years of being put on hold.
CAN REVAMPED RETEVISION COMPETE?

The question now is whether Retevision, a dumping ground for expensive state employees made redundant when Telefonica streamlined, can be made fit enough to stimulate the market and compete with the heavily armoured former state monopoly.
"It's a duopoly, but Telefonica is definitely going to be the stronger competitor," said a Spanish bank telecoms analyst.

The government, which is putting 51 percent of Retevision up for bid, has insisted the buyer be prepared to take on the 1,220 state workers, many of whom are former Telefonica engineers with costly pensions.
With a 18,000-km (11,000-mile) network, Retevision reaches 98 percent of the population by line of sight airwave, but lacks the local telecoms loop to homes and businesses.
"The key for Spanish telecoms is who wins the bid," Fernando Pardo, co-director of telecommunications at Price Waterhouse in Madrid, told Reuters.
The leading international contender is the Global One alliance of France Telecom, Germany's Deutsche Telekom and Sprint Corp of the United States, according to industry experts.
Britain's BT and Cable & Wireless as well as Italy's Stet STET.MI have also shown an interest. Domestically, a consortium formed by Endesa, BCH and Santander is likely to compete.

The new operator will have to link Retevision's extensive trunk network to clients either through interconnection with Telefonica, thus becoming its biggest client as well as its prime competitor, or through a deal with cable firms.
Pardo recommends that the Retevision operator reach a deal with Spain's fledgling cable operators to develop jointly a modern, high-tech network and avoid having two incomplete ones.
SPAIN LAGS IN CABLE COVER
Spain lags behind other European countries, except Italy, in cable coverage for television and other telecoms, reaching only 1.2 percent of homes in 1995.

Telefonica's attempt to redress the balance with a project with Canal Plus called Cablevision aimed to lay cable in high density areas but was scuppered by the European Commission on anti-trust grounds.
The operator then turned toward multimedia transmission by satellite and announced it was setting up a digital platform capable of distributing more than 100 channels.
But that agreement was dealt a serious blow last month when commercial television channel Antenna 3, with key rights to live soccer matches, moved to another satellite transmission project.
Industry experts meeting in Madrid last week said they were certain that the Telefonica of today would be able to respond to these latest ripples in the Spanish telecoms arena.

"Telefonica has a position as a de facto monopoly," Multitel chairman Eugenio Galdon said. "But what the consumers demand is what counts and what they demand is effective competition. That's what we're going to see."
